name: Drowned-Lullaby
description: Drowned-Lullaby is a world with no shores, its basalt seafloor buried beneath ninety kilometers of warm green ocean broken only by volcanic shoals and the endless slow spin of equatorial storm belts. The water glows: vast mats of luminous plankton trace currents like veins of light, brightest along the rift valleys where heat rises from below. From orbit at night the planet resembles a nervous system thinking in the dark.

The sea smells of rain and something sweeter, like overripe fruit, and the air carries a constant low thrum, the song of reef-glass whales rolling up through the water and into the hull of any visiting ship. Days are heavy and bright under high cirrus; nights belong to the glow, when whole ocean provinces flare blue-white as the great whale pods feed and sing. Swimmers report the light responding to their movements, rippling outward in answer.

The whales evolved here alone, engineers of the reef-glass structures that shelter the plankton mats, and for millennia the system ran in balance. Forty years ago deep-sea temperatures began climbing, driven by renewed rift volcanism, and the reef-glass started bleaching gray province by province. The orbital station that once monitored the die-off went dark six seasons ago; its support constellation has been drifting down into a decaying graveyard of dead satellites ever since.

Pharmaceutical guilds still pay fortunes for the whales' antiviral compounds, harvested ethically or otherwise, and salvage crews eye both the derelict station and whatever killed its crew. Conservation flotillas fight a rearguard action, seeding artificial reef-glass that the warming sea dissolves faster than it grows. The songs have grown shorter every year, and marine xenologists now argue openly about whether they are hearing a language winding down, or a countdown.
